excerpts: The idea behind the triple-barrier method is that we have three barriers: an upper barrier, a lower barrier, and a vertical barrier.

The upper barrier represents the threshold an observation’s return needs to reach in order to be considered a buying opportunity (a label of 1), the lower barrier represents the threshold an observation’s return needs to reach in order to be considered a selling opportunity (a label of -1), and the vertical barrier represents the amount of time an observation has to reach its given return in either direction before it is given a label of 0\.
This vertical barrier can be passed as an optional argument t1 in get\_events.

One of the major faults with the fixed-time horizon method is that observations are given a label with respect to a certain threshold after a fixed interval regardless of their respective volatilities. In other words, the expected returns of every observation are treated equally regardless of the associated risk. The triple-barrier method tackles this issue by dynamically setting the upper and lower barriers for each observation based on their given volatilities.

excerpts: (Note that the term has been used before (Lea et al., 2017).) The distinguishing characteristics of TCNs are: 1) the convolutions in the architecture are causal, meaning that there is no information “leakage” from future to past; 2) the architecture can take a sequence of any length and map it to an output sequence of the same length, just as with an RNN.
To achieve the second point, the TCN uses _causal convolutions_ , convolutions where an output at time _t_ is convolved only with elements from time _t_ and earlier in the previous layer.
The key constraint is that to predict the output _y_ _t_ for some time _t_ , we are constrained to only use those inputs that have been previously observed: _x_ 0 _, . . . , x_ _t_ .
Our solution here, following the work of van den Oord et al. (2016), is to employ dilated convolutions that enable an exponentially large receptive field (Yu & Koltun, 2016).
Using larger dilation enables an output at the top level to represent a wider range of inputs, thus effectively expanding the receptive field of a ConvNet.

This gives us two ways to increase the receptive field of the TCN: choosing larger filter sizes _k_ and increasing the dila- tion factor _d_ , where the effective history of one such layer is ( _k_ _−_ 1) _d_ .
As is common when using dilated convolutions, we increase _d_ exponentially with the depth of the network (i.e., _d_ = _O_ (2 _i_ ) at level _i_ of the network).

Beyond this, we emphasize how to build very long effective history sizes (i.e. , the ability for the networks to look very far into the past to make a prediction) using a combination of very deep networks (augmented with residual layers) and dilated convolutions.
These results indicate that TCNs are able to maintain a much longer effective history than their recurrent counterparts.
TCNs exhibit longer memory than recurrent architectures with the same capacity.
We compare the generic TCN architecture described in Sec- tion 3 to canonical recurrent architectures, namely LSTM, GRU, and vanilla RNN, with standard regularizations.
The experimental results indicate that TCN models substantially outperform generic recurrent ar- chitectures such as LSTMs and GRUs.
As shown in Table 1, TCN outperforms LSTMs and vanilla RNNs by a significant margin in perplex- ity on LAMBADA, with a substantially smaller network and virtually no tuning.

A major disadvantage of this basic design is that in order to achieve a long effective history size, we need an extremely deep network or very large filters, neither of which were particularly feasible when the methods were first introduced.
As previously noted, the generic TCN and LSTM/GRU models we used can be outperformed by more specialized architectures on some tasks.
The GLU does further improve TCN accuracy on certain language modeling datasets like PTB, which agrees with prior work.
However, we do not observe comparable benefits on other tasks, such as polyphonic music modeling or synthetic stress tests that require longer information retention.

excerpts: The idea behind the triple-barrier method is that we have three barriers: an upper barrier, a lower barrier, and a vertical barrier.

The upper barrier represents the threshold an observation’s return needs to reach in order to be considered a buying opportunity (a label of 1), the lower barrier represents the threshold an observation’s return needs to reach in order to be considered a selling opportunity (a label of -1), and the vertical barrier represents the amount of time an observation has to reach its given return in either direction before it is given a label of 0\.
This vertical barrier can be passed as an optional argument t1 in get\_events.

One of the major faults with the fixed-time horizon method is that observations are given a label with respect to a certain threshold after a fixed interval regardless of their respective volatilities. In other words, the expected returns of every observation are treated equally regardless of the associated risk. The triple-barrier method tackles this issue by dynamically setting the upper and lower barriers for each observation based on their given volatilities.

content.executive_summary:
- **Protect Convexity, Not Every Tick**: A Chandelier long stop is a high-water mark minus an ATR multiple, and the reference implementation uses 22 periods and 3 ATR on a daily chart [executive_summary[0]] [5] -> adapt the idea to 1-minute volatility, but do not copy daily parameters blindly.
- **Separate Stop Layers**: A hard initial stop, a profit floor, a trailing stop, a model exit, and a time stop answer different questions -> implement them as a state machine with one-way ratchets and explicit precedence.
- **Use R, Not Emotion**: Define 1R as the initial dollar risk plus realistic trading costs -> do not move to breakeven merely because a trade is slightly green; arm the first profit lock only after the observed excursion can statistically support it.
- **Let Trends Breathe**: Trailing stops can reduce investment risk without necessarily reducing investment losses [executive_summary[1]] [4] -> use a wider high-water-mark trail and a smaller scale-out in a confirmed trend.
- **Treat Scale-Out as Insurance**: A partial exit reduces exposure to give-back but sells part of the right tail -> compare its net expectancy and MFE capture with an all-in/all-out policy instead of optimizing win rate.
- **Use Two Exit Clocks**: A persistent signal flip says the thesis changed; a time stop says the trade failed to progress -> make the signal exit dominant after confirmation, and use a time stop mainly for stagnant positions.
- **Condition on Regime**: ADX measures trend strength rather than direction [executive_summary[2]] [14], while VWAP is a volume-weighted average price that can act as a dynamic reference [executive_summary[3]] [15] -> use trend evidence to choose a loose trail and mean-reversion evidence to choose faster targets.
- **Measure the Leak**: MAE is the worst move against the position and MFE is the best move in its favor [executive_summary[4]] [16][executive_summary[5]] [17] -> group results by MFE, MAE, regime, and exit reason before tightening a stop.
- **Align Labels With Execution**: Triple-barrier labeling uses upper, lower, and vertical time barriers [executive_summary[6]] [7] -> if live exits are dynamic, relabel or replay the actual policy rather than training on fixed barriers and deploying a different ratchet.
- **Respect 1-Minute Execution**: Crypto markets have limited depth and low update arrival rates relative with established markets [executive_summary[7]] [6], and OHLC bars can hide whether a stop or target was hit first [executive_summary[8]] [11] -> model bid/ask, latency, slippage, and intrabar order sequencing.
- **Failure Is Often Stop Design**: A published liquidation-bounce strategy made 205 trades, won 35.1%, and lost $1.3K [executive_summary[9]] [18]; 73 failures were attributed to stops that were too tight [executive_summary[9]] [18] -> do not cure profit give-back by making a valid 1-minute trail even tighter.

The exact constants below are a production starting grid, not a claim that every trading desk uses identical numbers. The public evidence supports the mechanisms and the failure modes; SOL/USDT-specific thresholds still require walk-forward calibration on the venue, fee tier, order type, and signal horizon.
content.why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit:
A TCN can be a sound causal signal engine without being an exit engine. The original TCN description requires causal convolutions, so the output at time t uses only time t and earlier inputs [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[0]] [8]. Dilations expand the receptive field [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[0]] [8], which is useful when a 1-minute model needs both recent order-flow pressure and a longer intraday context. But a forecast of next-bar direction does not specify how much adverse excursion is normal after a large favorable excursion, when the trend has ended, or how much execution cost a stop will incur.

The path from entry to exit matters. Crypto microstructure research identifies limited depth and low update arrival rates as differentiators from established markets [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[1]] [6], and finds that trade-flow imbalance and order-flow imbalance are related to contemporaneous price changes [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[1]] [6]. A profitable mark-to-market peak can therefore be followed by a fast retracement in which the bot's protective order consumes thin liquidity. The realized outcome is not simply the last close relative to the entry; it is the executable bid, spread, queue position, latency, and impact at the time the stop fires.

First separate the instrument. For spot SOL/USDT, the bot has bid/ask execution risk but no futures liquidation price. For a SOLUSDT perpetual, Binance states that Mark Price is calculated from funding data and a basket of spot prices [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[2]] [13], and that liquidation prices and unrealized PnL are based on Mark Price [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[2]] [13]. Do not use a chart's last-trade high-water mark and assume it is the price at which the position can be exited or liquidated.

Finally, a 1-minute OHLC backtest can manufacture good exits. When both a target and a stop fall inside one bar, the bar does not reveal the intrabar sequence; some engines impose an assumption such as Open-High-Low-Close [why_1_minute_sol_usdt_gives_back_profit[3]] [11]. Use trades or quotes where possible, or impose a conservative stop-first rule and then run a lower-timeframe sensitivity test.

**Decision:** treat profit give-back as a path and execution problem. The TCN supplies a probability or side; a separate, cost-aware exit controller owns risk, profit floors, and order state.
content.chandelier_and_atr_trails_that_preserve_:
For a long, the reference Chandelier formula is:

```text
raw_chandelier_t = highest_high_t(L) - k * ATR_t(N)
stop_t = max(stop_(t-1), raw_chandelier_t)
```

The documented default is a 22-period high, ATR(22), and multiplier 3 on a daily chart [chandelier_and_atr_trails_that_preserve_trend_convexity[0]] [5]. The source explains that the long exit hangs three ATR below the period high and can move as the high and ATR change [chandelier_and_atr_trails_that_preserve_trend_convexity[0]] [5]. The critical implementation detail is the `max`: once the long stop has risen, a volatility spike must not silently lower it. The short-side mirror is the period low plus ATR times the multiplier [chandelier_and_atr_trails_that_preserve_trend_convexity[0]] [5].

For a 1-minute SOL/USDT bot, use the formula as an architecture, not as a parameter prescription. A sensible initial calibration grid is ATR windows of 30, 60, and 120 one-minute bars, optionally computed on aggregated 5-minute bars, with trend multipliers of 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, and 4.0. That grid is deliberately broad. Select the smallest multiplier whose out-of-sample stop-out rate does not rise sharply in the intended trend regime, after costs. Do not choose it from the average winning trade or from the largest historical MFE.

Use a separate initial stop. Let `R` be the initial all-in dollar risk, including an estimate of entry and exit fees, spread, and slippage. For a long, maintain an economic floor in R terms and translate it into an exchange trigger with a slippage buffer:

```text
initial_stop = entry_price - initial_risk_distance
floor_price  = entry_price + locked_R * R_per_unit + cost_buffer
raw_trail    = executable_high_water_mark - k_regime * ATR_exit
candidate    = max(previous_stop, floor_price, raw_trail)
```

The high-water mark should be based on an executable bid or a conservative trade/quote proxy, not merely the candle high. Update the trail on a closed bar or a controlled quote event, but keep the protective order live between updates. Cap order-update frequency and use idempotent client order identifiers so a burst of 1-minute updates cannot leave duplicate or stale reduce-only orders.

| Position state | Proposed starter rule | What it protects | Main calibration test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial risk | Structure or volatility stop; never widen after entry | Catastrophic loss and model failure | Winner MAE and gap/slippage distribution |
| Not yet armed | No profit ratchet until a meaningful MFE threshold | Avoids locking noise before the trade proves itself | Conditional MAE after 0.5R, 0.75R, and 1R |
| Armed | Raise the floor only; never lower it | Converts a profitable path into a minimum economic outcome | Net P&L after stop fill degradation |
| Trend runner | High-water mark minus a wide ATR multiple | Preserves the right tail | MFE capture and trend continuation rate |
| Regime flip | Freeze the old floor, then tighten only after confirmation | Prevents one noisy classifier bar from changing policy | Two- or three-bar hysteresis test |

A volatility stop is not automatically safer when ATR expands. If the formula is allowed to loosen, a volatility shock can return an already protected trade to an unprotected state. If it is not allowed to loosen, the stop may be hit during a shock, which is appropriate if the shock has consumed the trade's previously earned risk budget. The distinction is intentional: a trailing stop protects accumulated equity; it is not a forecast of the next price.

**Decision:** implement `max(previous_stop, floor, high_water_mark - k * ATR)`. Calibrate `N`, `k`, and the arming threshold jointly by regime and net execution result; never optimize a 1-minute multiplier in isolation.
content.profit_locks_r_ratchets_and_scale_outs:
The cleanest way to stop a trade from going from a large unrealized gain to a token gain is to use a ratchet ladder rather than one instantaneous breakeven move. Let `MFE_R` be current peak unrealized profit measured in initial R, and let `locked_R` be the highest economic floor already earned. A long controller can use:

```text
if MFE_R >= 0.75 and locked_R < 0.00:
    locked_R = 0.00              # cost-adjusted breakeven, only if data supports it
if MFE_R >= 1.00 and locked_R < 0.10:
    locked_R = 0.10
if MFE_R >= 1.50 and locked_R < 0.25:
    locked_R = 0.25
if MFE_R >= 2.00 and locked_R < 0.50:
    locked_R = 0.50
locked_R = max(locked_R, prior_locked_R)
```

These numbers are starter values, not universal standards. The default I would test for a noisy 1-minute SOL/USDT system is no exact breakeven before 1R unless the conditional MAE study supports an earlier lock. At minimum, breakeven must include expected round-trip fees, spread, and slippage. An exchange fill below the trigger can still turn a nominal breakeven into a loss, so call it a cost-adjusted floor, not a guarantee.

A useful worked example is a hypothetical SOL/USDT TCN long, expressed only in R. The position begins with a -1R initial stop, reaches +3R MFE, and then retraces. With no ratchet, it can exit at +0.1R. With a ladder that earned +0.25R at 1.5R and +0.5R at 2R, the same path exits at or above the floor, subject to slippage. The example is not a historical trade and proves no optimal threshold; it shows why the controller must remember the peak state instead of recomputing a fresh stop from the current price.

Scale-out is a different tool. A simple candidate is 25% to 33% at 1R, another 25% to 33% at 2R, and 34% to 50% as the runner. An alternative is 33% at 1R and 67% under a trend trail. Compare these against all-in/all-out using the same signals and the same fills. For a fraction `q` taken at target `T`, the gross path outcome is approximately:

```text
scaled_outcome = q * T + (1 - q) * runner_exit
```

The early partial improves the outcome when the runner would have given back enough, but it reduces the payoff when the trend continues. It can also inflate win rate while lowering average win and right-tail capture. Keep R defined from the original full-position risk so that a partial does not make the trade appear safer merely because the remaining size is smaller.

A practical compromise for a trend-following TCN is a small insurance partial and a large runner; for a mean-reversion signal, a larger target partial and a smaller or zero runner. Do not add a partial simply because the equity curve looks uncomfortable. Require it to improve net expectancy, drawdown, turnover-adjusted Sharpe, and the distribution of MFE capture in a walk-forward test.

**Decision:** use an R-based, one-way profit floor first; add scale-outs only when counterfactual replay shows that the reduction in give-back outweighs the right-tail revenue surrendered.
content.signal_flip_time_stop_and_regime_aware_e:
The exit controller should not let five independent rules fight over one order. Use this priority for a long:

1. Venue, liquidation, and portfolio emergency controls.
2. Initial hard stop or already-earned economic floor.
3. Confirmed model signal flip or structural invalidation.
4. Target and scale-out events.
5. Time stop for failure to progress.
6. Chandelier runner trail.

The exact order between a confirmed signal flip and a pre-existing profit floor depends on the mandate. A risk-first desk should exit when the model invalidates, while a trend mandate may let the runner remain if the flip is only one noisy bar. The key is to specify the policy before seeing the path.

Use hysteresis for the TCN output. For example, if `p_long` is the calibrated probability of a favorable long outcome, do not exit because it moves from 0.54 to 0.49 for one bar. Test a rule such as `p_long < 0.45` for two consecutive bars, or a larger negative probability change combined with a price/structure break. Calibrate the threshold to precision, turnover, and post-signal MFE, not to accuracy alone.

A time stop is not a substitute for a weak signal. It answers whether the position has used its opportunity window. A defensible starter policy is: after 10 to 15 one-minute bars with MFE below 0.25R, reduce or close the position; after 60 to 120 bars, close any remaining position unless the signal is still strong and the trend regime is confirmed. Extend the runner only after it has earned at least 1R and has a valid trailing floor. These numbers must be selected from the empirical hold-time and MFE curves.

A preliminary study in another intraday context reports that time-aware exit rules better preserved intraday breakout signals than price-based stops at volume-defined boundaries [signal_flip_time_stop_and_regime_aware_exit_arbitration[0]] [12]. That is useful directional evidence, not proof for SOL/USDT. It supports testing a time stop as a separate policy rather than forcing every exit through a price stop.

| Exit | Best use | What it avoids | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confirmed signal flip | Thesis or direction has changed | Staying in a decaying edge | One-bar noise and model churn |
| Time stop | Position has not progressed | Capital trapped in stale trades | Cutting a slow trend before expansion |
| Chandelier | Trend has earned a runner | Fixed target truncating the right tail | Too tight for 1-minute noise |
| Profit floor | Large MFE has been earned | Returning to a tiny gain or loss | Floor triggered before the trade has proven itself |
| Scale-out | Reduce exposure to give-back | Entire position reverses | Selling too much of a continuing trend |

**Decision:** make signal flips thesis exits, time stops opportunity-cost exits, and trails path-protection exits. Do not allow a generic time limit or one-bar probability wiggle to override a tested regime-specific policy.
content.regime_aware_trailing_trend_versus_mean_:
A single trail cannot serve two different payoff shapes. Trend following expects continuation after a favorable move, so its opportunity cost is selling too early. Mean reversion expects a move back toward a reference level, so its opportunity cost is holding after the reversion has already occurred or after the premise has failed.

Use features available at the decision time only. A trend state can require an aligned EMA slope, price holding on the favorable side of session or anchored VWAP, rising ADX, and a sequence of higher highs and higher lows. EMA puts more weight on recent observations [regime_aware_trailing_trend_versus_mean_reversion[0]] [19]. VWAP is volume-weighted and can act as a dynamic support or resistance reference [regime_aware_trailing_trend_versus_mean_reversion[1]] [15]. ADX measures strength rather than direction [regime_aware_trailing_trend_versus_mean_reversion[2]] [14], so direction must come from the price/EMA/VWAP alignment.

Use rolling percentiles instead of assuming that a fixed ADX or ATR number transfers from BTC to SOL or from one venue to another. Require two or three bars of confirmation to enter a new regime and use hysteresis so the bot does not switch trail multipliers on every 1-minute oscillation. A high-volatility shock is a third state, not automatically a trend state: widen the initial risk only before entry, reduce size, and do not add to a position while the stop is being mechanically recalculated.

| Regime | Detection template | Trail and floor | Exit bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confirmed trend | EMA slope and VWAP side aligned; ADX above its rolling percentile; directional closes persist | `k = 3.0 to 4.0` starter grid; small partial; runner uses Chandelier | Wait for confirmed flip or trail; avoid fixed full take-profit |
| Mean reversion | ADX below rolling percentile; price stretched from VWAP; reversion features dominate | `k = 1.5 to 2.5` starter grid; take 50% to 75% near the reference/target; faster floor | Exit into the reference or on a confirmed invalidation |
| Volatility shock | ATR percentile spikes; spread or depth deteriorates; signal confidence unstable | Do not loosen an earned floor; reduce new risk and use conservative fills | Emergency and invalidation rules dominate |
| Uncertain transition | Trend and mean-reversion votes disagree | Freeze the last floor; do not tighten on one bar; reduce size if policy permits | Time stop or confirmed flip |

The ranges are deliberately presented as a calibration grid. The right answer may be outside them, and a tighter mean-reversion trail can still be wrong if SOL/USDT spreads and latency consume the edge. The state machine should record the regime at entry and at every exit so that a profitable trend trade stopped by a mean-reversion policy is visible as a policy mismatch rather than blamed on the TCN.

**Decision:** choose the exit policy from the payoff distribution expected by the regime. Trend mode protects the runner; mean-reversion mode monetizes the destination; transition mode avoids sudden tightening.
content.mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_l:
MAE/MFE analysis turns the give-back anecdote into measurable conditional data. For a long with initial risk distance `R_price`, compute:

```text
MAE_R = max((entry_price - executable_low_t) / R_price)
MFE_R = max((executable_high_t - entry_price) / R_price)
giveback_R = MFE_R - realized_exit_R
capture    = realized_exit_R / MFE_R       # only when MFE_R > 0
```

Use executable-side prices and record the timestamp of the peak, not just the final bar. The usual definitions are path-based: MAE is the largest adverse move before exit [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[0]] [16], and MFE is the furthest favorable move while open [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[1]] [17]. Add time-to-MFE, time-to-MAE, spread, slippage, regime, model probability, entry reason, and exit reason.

Then make four conditional plots or tables: winners versus losers by MAE, realized P&L versus MFE, give-back versus time since peak, and all three by regime. Interpret them as follows:

- If eventual winners routinely reach 0.6R MAE before moving, a 0.25R initial stop is a noise filter, not risk control.
- If trades that reach 2R MFE usually finish above 1R but the bot exits near 0R, the exit controller is leaking value.
- If trades with 2R MFE later reverse into losses only after a regime flip, a signal exit or a two-stage ratchet is more appropriate than a permanently tighter trail.
- If high-MFE trades still give back after realistic costs, the entry model may predict a temporary impulse rather than a tradable trend.

These are decision rules, not universal empirical laws. Estimate thresholds on a training window, freeze them, and validate on a later window. Do not use the same sample both to discover a peak-MFE threshold and to claim that it improved performance. Stop-loss research in momentum strategies has found ambiguous statistical significance, with results becoming mixed after data-snooping controls such as White's Reality Check [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[2]] [3].

Triple-barrier labeling supplies a useful baseline. It uses an upper profit-taking barrier, a lower stop-loss barrier, and a vertical time barrier [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[3]] [7]. Its implementation can set the horizontal barrier widths from a volatility target rather than from one fixed percentage [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[3]] [7], and `pt_sl` explicitly represents profit-taking and stop-loss multiples [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[3]] [7]. Meta-labeling can incorporate the primary model's side and let a secondary model decide whether to take or pass the bet [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[3]] [7].

The implication for a dynamic live exit is direct:

1. If the bot is trained to predict a fixed upper/lower/time outcome, evaluate it with that same policy.
2. If live execution uses a Chandelier ratchet, dynamic profit floors, and partials, generate labels with a path replay of that policy or train separate targets for side, MFE bucket, time-to-barrier, and exit reason.
3. For scale-outs, label net position P&L after the partial schedule, not just whether the high reached a single upper barrier.
4. Make barriers cost-aware. A nominal `+0.2R` outcome that is smaller than fees, spread, and expected stop slippage should not be a positive label.
5. Keep future MFE and future barrier touches in the label only. Features supplied to the causal TCN must be lagged and available at entry; otherwise causal convolutions do not rescue a leaky feature pipeline.

Because event labels overlap in time, use purged and embargoed time-series validation; a time-series cross-validation reference describes these methods as preventing leakage through proper purging and embargo [mae_mfe_diagnostics_and_triple_barrier_labeling[4]] [20].

**Decision:** use MAE/MFE to calibrate stops and diagnose exit leakage, and use triple barriers only when their barriers represent the policy the bot will actually execute.
content.sol_usdt_tcn_bot_implementation_and_fail:
Keep the TCN and the exit manager separate. The TCN can output `p_long`, an uncertainty score, and optionally an MFE or time-to-event estimate. The exit manager owns state, fills, and risk. The original TCN work supports causal history and dilated receptive fields [sol_usdt_tcn_bot_implementation_and_failure_controls[0]] [8], but also warns that long effective histories may require a very deep network or large filters [sol_usdt_tcn_bot_implementation_and_failure_controls[0]] [8]. A larger receptive field is not a reason to use a longer holding time or a wider stop.

A production-oriented controller can be expressed as:

```text
on_entry:
    R = initial_dollar_risk + expected_round_trip_cost
    state = INITIAL
    stop = initial_stop
    hwm = executable_bid
    submit_reduce_only_protective_stop(stop)

on_each_quote_or_closed_bar:
    update_hwm_from_executable_bid()
    update_MAE_MFE_in_initial_R()
    p_long = TCN_probability_using_only_lagged_features()
    regime = regime_classifier_with_hysteresis()

    if venue_or_portfolio_emergency:
        flatten_reduce_only()
    elif state == INITIAL and MFE_R >= arm_threshold:
        state = ARMED
        locked_R = first_floor_from_MAE_MFE_table()
    elif MFE_R crosses_next_ladder_level:
        locked_R = max(locked_R, next_cost_adjusted_floor())

    chandelier = hwm - k(regime) * ATR_exit
    desired_stop = max(stop, chandelier, price_for_floor(locked_R))

    if confirmed_signal_flip(p_long, regime, persistence):
        exit_or_reduce_by_policy()
    elif time_stop_without_progress():
        exit_or_reduce_by_policy()
    else:
        replace_or_amend_reduce_only_stop(desired_stop)

on_fill_or_reconnect:
    reconcile_exchange_position_and_open_orders()
    cancel_duplicates()
    restore_protective_stop_before_new_entry()
```

For 1-minute SOL/USDT, log at least: venue and symbol type, bid/ask, last, mark if applicable, spread, depth proxy, ATR window, high-water mark, current and peak MFE, MAE, locked floor, regime, TCN probability, signal persistence, order submission time, acknowledgment time, trigger time, fill price, slippage, and exit reason. This makes a token profit after a 3R peak distinguishable from a stop design failure, a latency failure, a signal flip, or a bad bar simulation.

Backtest three layers separately: signal-only mark-to-market, executable fill simulation, and live-like order-state simulation. For each, run stop-first and target-first intrabar assumptions, then lower-timeframe replay. Include fees, spread, slippage, partial-fill probability, latency, and rejected or stale order handling. For a perpetual, monitor the venue's mark-price and liquidation conventions rather than treating last price as the sole risk variable [sol_usdt_tcn_bot_implementation_and_failure_controls[1]] [13].

Do not tune the exit on a single SOL/USDT bull run. Use rolling walk-forward periods, purged validation for overlapping labels, and a parameter surface rather than one winning point. A TCN result can look strong on prediction metrics while the executable exit is negative after turnover and impact; the research on crypto order flow and limited depth makes that gap especially relevant [sol_usdt_tcn_bot_implementation_and_failure_controls[2]] [6].

**Decision:** make the exit manager a deterministic, testable component with its own metrics and failure budget. A good TCN signal cannot compensate for a non-idempotent stop, a leaky label, or an optimistic 1-minute fill model.
content.case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failur:
A published liquidation-cascade strategy monitors liquidation-volume spikes together with sharp open-interest drops [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18], then enters a long bounce after liquidation velocity declines [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18]. Its backtest used hourly OHLCV data across more than 65 symbols, an initial $10K balance, 0.1% commission, and 0.05% slippage [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18]. Over 205 trades, it produced a 35.1% win rate and lost $1,300 [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18].

The failure taxonomy is more useful than the headline loss. It attributed 73 trades to a stop that was too tight even though the bounce attempt was genuine, 21 to an adverse move because the cascade was not actually over, and 19 to low-volatility chop and false positives [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18]. The author concludes that the concept has merit but needs better cascade-end detection, post-cascade stops, and differentiation between a bounce and the beginning of a larger downturn [case_study_the_liquidation_bounce_failure[0]] [18].

This is not a SOL/USDT 1-minute result, so it should not be used to select a SOL multiplier. It is a clean case study of the exact diagnostic split needed here. A trade can be directionally right but stopped by an overly narrow trail; it can be a false exhaustion signal; or it can be a valid signal whose market regime changes. Tightening every stop treats all three as the same problem and usually makes the first category worse.

For a TCN bot, replay these categories with MAE/MFE and exit reason. If the 73-type cluster exists, widen the post-entry trail or delay arming. If the 21-type cluster exists, improve signal confirmation or regime filters. If the 19-type cluster exists, add a no-trade or minimum-volatility condition. Do not ask the exit to fix an entry that never had a tradable edge.

**Decision:** classify the loss before changing the stop. Profit give-back is an exit problem only when the entry path had enough conditional MFE to justify a different exit.
content.synthesis:
| Mechanism | Primary job | Best horizon or regime | Advantage | Main trade-off and failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial ATR/structure stop | Cap adverse entry risk | All regimes | Simple, auditable, position-size compatible | Too close to 1-minute noise; too wide increases loss |
| Profit-lock ratchet | Preserve an earned minimum | After meaningful MFE | Stops a 3R path from becoming a token gain | Early lock truncates trades that need room |
| Chandelier trail | Monetize a trend high-water mark | Persistent trend | Keeps the right tail open | Overtight multiplier gets shaken out; ATR can be miscalibrated |
| Scale-out | Exchange tail for lower variance | Mean reversion or uncertain trend | Reduces exposure to give-back | Sells profitable continuation and adds turnover |
| Signal-flip exit | Respond to thesis decay | Model-driven directional trade | Can exit before a price stop | Probability noise causes churn without hysteresis |
| Time stop | Release stale capital | No-progress or bounded-horizon signal | Prevents indefinite holds | Can cut slow trends before expansion |
| Triple-barrier label | Define a supervised outcome | Fixed or explicitly simulated policy | Connects target, stop, and time in one label | Mismatch with dynamic live exits creates training error |

The central tension is not whether to trail. It is what the bot believes a favorable excursion means. In trend mode, a large MFE may be evidence that the trade has entered a new payoff regime, so the correct response is a wider ratchet and a smaller partial. In mean-reversion mode, the same MFE may mean the target has already been reached, so retaining a full runner adds reversal risk. A single global trail hides this distinction.

The second tension is protection versus evidence. A breakeven rule feels safe, but a 1-minute position can be profitable in direction and still need a normal MAE before continuation. The trailing-stop study's distinction between reducing investment risk and reducing investment losses [synthesis[0]] [4] is the right warning: a stop can lower variance without improving expectancy. The only defensible trigger is the conditional MAE/MFE distribution after costs.

The third tension is model versus execution. The TCN is causal by construction [synthesis[1]] [8], but labels, features, bars, and fills can still leak future information or overstate liquidity. Triple-barrier labels are valuable precisely because they make the exit horizon explicit [synthesis[2]] [7]; they become dangerous when the model is trained on fixed barriers and deployed with a dynamic ratchet.

What the research establishes is the architecture, the execution risks, and the diagnostic method. What it does not establish is a universal SOL/USDT answer for ATR length, multiplier, breakeven R, scale-out fraction, or time stop. Those remain empirical policy parameters. The recommended next experiment is a four-way walk-forward comparison using identical entries: all-in Chandelier, R-ratchet plus runner, partial plus runner, and signal/time arbitration. Rank them by net expectancy, tail capture, drawdown, turnover, stop-out after MFE, and fill slippage, not by win rate or the largest unrealized peak.

**Decision:** deploy the simplest policy that preserves a tested fraction of MFE at acceptable cost, and change one exit layer at a time. Never solve a label mismatch, liquidity problem, or false signal by merely tightening the trailing stop.
